questions.question: 安德森说民族是「想象的共同体」，他与把民族的「发明」等同于「捏造」的看法有什么不同？
options: 民族是古老族群在近代被唤醒了自我意识，「想象」指的是重新发现已有的认同
民族是精英为了统治目的而捏造的虚假意识，「想象」就是要揭穿它背后并不存在真实的共同体
民族的想象一旦发生便不再需要维护，所以它比宗教、亲属这类纽带更稳固
任何大过面对面村庄的共同体都只能靠想象存在，共同体的区别不在真伪，而在被想象的方式
questions.explanation: 安德森同意民族是现代发明，但批评把「发明」悄悄等同于「捏造」，仿佛背后还有一个真共同体可以对照；他要问的是人们用报纸、地图、日历等什么具体手段去想象。「精英骗局」与「古老民族被唤醒」恰是他两头都否定的说法。
questions.question_en: Anderson calls the nation an 'imagined community'. How does this differ from the view that treats the 'invention' of nations as 'fabrication'?
options_en: Nations are ancient peoples whose self-awareness was awakened in modern times, and 'imagined' means rediscovering an existing identity
The nation is a false consciousness fabricated by elites to rule, and 'imagined' exposes that no real community stands behind it
Once a nation has been imagined it no longer needs maintaining, which makes it sturdier than religious or kinship ties
Any community larger than a face-to-face village can exist only through imagination; communities differ not by being genuine or false but by the style in which they are imagined
questions.explanation_en: Anderson agrees nations are modern inventions but faults the slide from 'invention' to 'fabrication', as if a genuine community lay behind it for comparison; his question is what concrete means — newspapers, maps, calendars — people use to imagine it. 'Elite hoax' and 'ancient nation awakened' are the two positions he rejects.

questions.question: 西属美洲独立时没有成为一个大国，而是沿着殖民行政区的边界碎成十几个国家。安德森如何解释？
options: 安第斯山脉等地理屏障阻断了交通往来，各地区被险峻的地形彼此隔开，只能各自建国
西班牙王室有意分而治之，在独立之前就为每个地区分别培养了各自的民族意识
仕途被封顶在本行政区内，同行者都是本区人，加上本地小报，行政区就被想成了祖国
各地区说着不同的语言和方言，语言的边界自然而然地划出了后来国家的边界
questions.explanation: 这些新国家和宗主国说同一种语言，语言解释不了它们。安德森借「朝圣」概念：美洲出生的克里奥尔官员几乎升不到马德里，一辈子在同一行政区里流动，共同被封顶的命运让他们把这块地方想成「我们的」，殖民者画的行政线于是成了想象的边界。
questions.question_en: At independence, Spanish America did not become one large state but broke into a dozen countries along colonial administrative lines. How does Anderson explain this?
options_en: Geographic barriers such as the Andes cut off travel, so each region was isolated by terrain and had to found its own state
The Spanish crown deliberately divided and ruled, cultivating a separate national consciousness in each region before independence
Creole careers were capped within their own administrative unit, their fellow travellers were all from that unit, and with local newspapers the unit came to be imagined as the homeland
The regions spoke different languages and dialects, and linguistic boundaries naturally drew the national borders
questions.explanation_en: These new states spoke the same language as the metropole, so language can't explain them. Borrowing the idea of pilgrimage, Anderson notes that American-born creole officials almost never rose to Madrid and spent their careers circulating within one unit; their shared ceiling made them imagine that territory as 'ours', so colonial administrative lines became imagined borders.

questions.question: 安德森认为报纸对想象民族最关键的是什么？
options: 头版日期把不相干的新闻并列为「今天」，读者确信无数陌生人此刻在读同样的东西
报纸让读者第一次见到远方同胞的照片和名字，从而真正认识了彼此
报纸记录民族的古老历史，让读者看到同胞跨越几百年的连续传承
社论有计划地宣传民族主义观点，报社编辑部是自上而下塑造民族意识的指挥中心所在
questions.explanation: 报纸凭「都发生在今天」把旱灾、议会、谋杀放在同一页，读报成了「晨祷」式的群众仪式，体现的是同质、空洞的「与此同时」。文中强调这一切没有人刻意策划，民族是印刷资本主义的意外结果；读者也恰恰不知道其他读者是谁。
questions.question_en: According to Anderson, what is the most important thing a newspaper does for imagining the nation?
options_en: The date on the front page binds unrelated stories together as 'today', and each reader is confident thousands of strangers are reading the same thing right now
It shows readers photos and names of distant compatriots for the first time, so they actually get to know one another
It records the nation's ancient history, showing readers an unbroken lineage of compatriots across centuries
Its editorials systematically promote nationalist views, making the newsroom the command centre of national consciousness
questions.explanation_en: The paper puts a drought, a parliamentary debate and a murder on one page simply because they all happened 'today'; reading it becomes a mass ceremony like a 'morning prayer', expressing homogeneous, empty time and 'meanwhile'. Anderson stresses no one planned this — the nation was an unintended result of print capitalism — and readers precisely do not know who the others are.
